articles.title: Justina Shiroka Pula: Kosovo’s new president, elected during a crisis
articles.summary: An academic, former minister and a compromise choice, Pula was voted in by parliament amid protests.
articles.body:
Kosovo’s election of a new president has brought an end to heightened tensions in parliament and possibly on the streets.

On Tuesday, protests against the convictions of former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders coincided with a midnight deadline to elect a president.

Ultimately, the ruling Vetevendosje Movement (LVV) and opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) reached an agreement on her candidacy, clearing the way for a parliamentary vote.

Lawmakers elected Justina Shiroka Pula to the country’s top office in the first minutes of Wednesday, close to the constitutional deadline, averting new early parliamentary elections that could have pushed the country into a deeper crisis.

The 81 votes she secured – one more than the two-thirds, 80-vote threshold required – were the result of a pragmatic compromise.

The parties also agreed to adopt amendments changing the legal framework governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the Hague-based court established to try former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders for alleged war crimes – an issue demonstrators had been urging politicians to address.

After a prolonged period of political deadlock, none of Kosovo’s political parties appeared willing to take responsibility for triggering another election.

“I see the election of Justina Shiroka Pula as a mix of political necessity and the need to stabilise institutions,” Donika Emini, a research fellow at the University of Graz’s Centre for Southeast European Studies, told Al Jazeera.

Kosovo had already been in a prolonged political limbo, she said, with election fatigue and increasing public dissatisfaction with the political elite.

After the Specialist Chambers verdict and 20 days of protests, including violent incidents in Pristina on the night before the presidential vote, “going into yet another election would have carried a high political cost for everyone,” Emini said.

“I see this as more than a temporary fix, but I wouldn’t read it as proof that the underlying polarisation has been resolved.

“It was, above all, a politically necessary compromise to restore institutional functioning.”

Who is Shiroka Pula, Kosovo’s third woman president?

Shiroka Pula’s election extends the run of women leading Kosovo. The 73-year-old is the country’s third female president, after Atifete Jahjaga and Vjosa Osmani.

Born in Pristina in 1953, Shiroka Pula brings to the presidency a career spanning academia, public institutions and politics.

After graduating from the University of Pristina’s economics faculty, she completed postgraduate studies in the theory and policy of economic development at the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb, then in Yugoslavia. She later earned a doctorate, researching the relationship between demographic investment and Kosovo’s economic development.

After a brief period working at the National Bank of Kosovo, Shiroka Pula began a long academic career back at the University of Pristina, rising from assistant lecturer to professor and heading the department of management and informatics.

Last December, she became the first woman to be elected head of the Kosovo Academy of Sciences and Arts, known by its Albanian acronym ASHAK.

Her path to the presidency, however, has not been solely academic.

Shiroka Pula served as Kosovo’s minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011. She was then a PDK member of parliament from 2011 to 2014.

That record means she should not be portrayed simply as a non-partisan academic, Emini said.

“She has a substantial political and institutional background,” Emini told Al Jazeera. “She was minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011 and a PDK member of the Assembly from 2011 to 2014.

“She has also had a long academic career and has worked extensively with civil society, which in Kosovo had an extensive state-building role for a long period of time,” Emini added.

The combination gives Shiroka Pula a strong understanding of Kosovo’s political and institutional landscape, as well as experience that could allow her to act as a counterbalance between institutions.

Her name was already acceptable to different political actors and was seen as less confrontational than other prospective candidates, according to Emini.

“The outcome was driven by urgency, but it also opens an opportunity to move Kosovo out of a long period of institutional paralysis,” she said.

Unlike the previous presidential arrangement, Shiroka Pula begins her term with backing from the ruling LVV and the PDK, giving her a broad political base from the outset.

But the extent of her political room for manoeuvre will depend on the relationships she develops with the Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) and other opposition parties, as well as on the team she assembles in her office.

“The question is less whether she has that experience and more whether she will have the political courage and institutional backing to use it independently,” Emini said.

Hopes for a ‘more coordinated’ leadership

Kosovo’s president has limited formal executive powers. Yet the office carries political and diplomatic weight: The president represents the country at home and abroad, helps safeguard institutional continuity, and can mediate when relations between political parties are blocked.

Shiroka Pula’s academic, institutional and international exposure may also make her an appealing figure to Kosovo’s international partners, Emini said. But her influence will depend on how she uses the political and diplomatic space offered by the office, and on her relationship with the government.

Historically, Kosovo’s presidents have at times played a more active foreign policy role than the constitutional division of responsibilities might suggest, depending on the individual and on their relationship with the prime minister.

“I hope this presidency will bring a more coordinated foreign policy among the president, the prime minister and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” Emini said. “The tensions between the previous president and the government showed how costly poor inter-institutional coordination can be, including on important processes such as Kosovo’s Council of Europe membership.”

articles.title: French school riots deepen as experts point to far-left alliance fueling ‘broader confrontation’
articles.summary: French student protests over school conditions spiral into violent unrest, as experts warn a red-green alliance is fueling a broader revolt,
articles.body: An unholy alliance is being blamed for instigating the violence seen across France as experts point to a bond between extreme left and radical Islamic groups. What began as protests over school conditions and funding is entering its third week, and the factors behind the widespread, more violent protests are being debated. "The protests started in an apparently spontaneous way in the disadvantaged, immigrant suburbs of Paris," Nathalie Szerman, researcher in radicalization and extremism in France at MEMRI, told Fox News Digital, but "it quickly became clear that the violence demonstrated in these protests conveyed a huge amount of hate towards the ‘system’ and not much concern for better material conditions in schools, as dozens of schools across France have suffered vandalism and blockades, and many were even set on fire." FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE Szerman said that while demonstrations over school conditions at the beginning of an academic year in France "is not a new phenomenon," the "scope of these demonstrations and their character should raise concerns." She points to protestors taking to the streets carrying Palestinian flags. "Pro-Palestinian organizations, such as Urgence Palestine, have declared the month of October to be a month of revolt, and these groups are supporting and fueling these demonstrations." "I think at the very heart of this, is the far-left and the Islamists combining forces to undermine France itself." "The French are notorious for strikes, labor shortages and street demonstrations," former U.S. Assistant Attorney General Theo Wold told Fox News Digital, and added that these protests are "a consequence of mass immigration. The rioters are not of French culture, and they don’t respect the rule of law … France is learning that importing an underclass of foreigners causes broader societal damage." ISRAELI AMBASSADOR COMPARES FRANCE'S FAR-LEFT LEADER'S RHETORIC TO HITLER AS ANTISEMITISM SURGES Nile Gardiner, director of The Heritage Foundation's Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom, told Fox News’ Outnumbered on Tuesday, "I think at the very heart of this, is the far-left and the Islamists combining forces to undermine France itself … This is a form of uprising, frankly, by far left wing forces together with second, third generation migrants. And also, at the same time, France is in real economic trouble." Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that, "Students have reason to be angry about overcrowded classrooms and absent teachers." She added: "What does Gaza have to do with a shortage of teachers in France? I’ll tell you what: [the far-left La France Insoumise party] has spent years making hostility to Israel a central part of its appeal to young voters. Bringing that cause into the school protests helps fuel the racial dynamics and turn a demand for better classrooms into a much broader confrontation with the government," she said. EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT "LFI is the perfect embodiment of the Red-Green alliance – the alliance between leftists and Islamists," added Szerman. "LFI rallies Islamist and pro-Palestinian groups on the one hand, and other French anti-system leftists who accuse the elite of enriching itself at the expense of the poor on the other. It is a revolutionary party using Islam as an inner drive. Politicized Muslims are aware of this and are also using LFI to promote their own agenda. "They are fueling and empowering each other, the common ground being the claim that they are the people," Szerman continued. "The people are seen as the enemy of the ‘elite’ running the country, which therefore has to be overthrown." Rodan-Benzaquen said, "French students need their teachers to show up to class, and their parents need to know they will be safe at school. But [LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon] is not interested in these goals." She says he is "encouraging the citizens to see their schools as a front in a larger political battle, one whose real prize is the presidency." FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT French President Emmanuel Macron is term-limited and cannot run for a third consecutive term in elections this coming spring. Many observers believe a runoff match-up between the far-left Mélenchon and right-wing populist Marine Le Pen of the National Rally party could be on the horizon. "No matter how the protests play out, Mélenchon will likely benefit," said Rodan-Benzaquen. "If the unrest drives voters toward the far right, he can hope to emerge as the leader of the opposition. If he succeeds in mobilizing enough voters himself, he could reach the presidency. Either prospect gives him a reason to keep the confrontation going. Neither gives him much incentive to lower the temperature." "I do not think that the LFI leadership made a conscious decision to trigger destructive demonstrations all over France," added Szerman, "but once the movement was launched, LFI did provide a backbone for the violence, as it will never blame any of its followers." FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION So far, the protests have not spread across the continent even as spending on education seems close between countries. According to the latest available figures from Eurostat, the European Union’s official statistical office, in 2024 France spent over 5% of its GDP on education, more than it spent on defense. In that same year, neighboring Germany spent only 4.5% of its GDP on education.In Macron’s latest proposed budget, about $74 billion is earmarked for French schools, more than proposed for defense, but both are cuts from the last official budget narrowly approved by Parliament over the winter. Germany’s Federal Statistical Office reports spending on education was up to 7% of GDP at over $340 billion when including federal, state and local government spending. Meanwhile, in the U.K., Department for Education spending for the 2025/26 school year was estimated at around $142 billion. When comparing the latest figures for expenditures per student, France’s ministry of education says in the 2024/25 school year, it spent $9,950 per student, Germany’s Federal Statistical Office says $12,000 was spent per student in 2025, and the U.K. spent about $10,100 per student in 2024/25. Meanwhile, the Organization for European Economic Co-operation says the Europe-wide average is around $12,000 per student per year. Some 500 high schools are closed in France on Wednesday, down from 891 on Tuesday. The schools have been ordered by the ministry of education to replace normal lessons through Friday with structured dialogue and staff crisis management meetings in an effort to calm tensions, to avoid confrontations at school gates and to give staff time to reorganize. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Associated Press reports more than 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, with the Interior Ministry saying 715 police officers have been injured.

articles.title: King Charles visited a project testing contraceptives on grey squirrels; the unusual plan aims to save Britain's rare red squirrels
articles.summary: King Charles visited a research project in North Yorkshire exploring a new way to control Britain's grey squirrel population and help protect its native
articles.body: King Charles visited a research project in North Yorkshire exploring a new way to control Britain's grey squirrel population and help protect its native red squirrels. During his visit on May 26, 2026, the King met scientists at the Animal and Plant Health Agency's York Biotech Campus in Sand Hutton and learned about research into an oral contraceptive for grey squirrels. The approach is designed to reduce reproduction rather than rely only on conventional population control. Grey squirrels are an introduced species that competes with red squirrels for food and living space. They also carry squirrelpox, a virus that is usually fatal to reds. Researchers are developing a targeted feeding system to deliver the contraceptive to greys while keeping red squirrels and other wildlife out.King Charles sees unusual squirrel projectDuring the visit, Charles met the Animal and Plant Health Agency's wildlife scientists and saw how the contraceptive, which is delivered in a hazelnut paste, is developed. Dr Julie Lane, head of the agency's National Wildlife Management Centre, told him: "Without you, this work would not be happening at all." She later said the King was very interested in the work, particularly because of his love for red squirrels. The project is part of wider research into non-lethal ways of managing grey squirrel populations. Charles, patron of the Red Squirrel Survival Trust, has championed red squirrel conservation for decades.Why grey squirrels are being targetedGrey squirrels were introduced to Britain from North America in the 19th century and have since spread across much of the country. The UK government estimates that Great Britain now has around 2.7 million of them. Greys are generally unaffected by squirrelpox, but the virus is usually fatal to red squirrels. They also strip bark from trees, damaging woodland.Britain's red squirrels are now rareRed squirrels are Britain's only native squirrel species, yet only an estimated 120,000 to 160,000 remain, most of them in Scotland. They have disappeared from much of mainland England and Wales, with important populations surviving in parts of northern England, Scotland, Wales and on several islands. Their decline has been linked to competition from greys, squirrelpox and habitat loss. The Eurasian red squirrel is classified as Least Concern globally by the IUCN, but its range in Britain has contracted so sharply that local conservation measures matter greatly.Scientists are developing an oral contraceptiveThe research programme, led by the Animal and Plant Health Agency and funded by the UK Squirrel Accord, is developing an oral immunocontraceptive vaccine. Rather than capturing animals individually, scientists hope to incorporate the treatment into bait distributed through specialised feeders, gradually lowering grey squirrel numbers. The vaccine works by preventing an animal's immune system from producing sex hormones. Agency researchers have achieved infertility in rats fed the oral formulation, a world first for wildlife fertility control. In grey squirrels the formulation has so far produced an immune response but not infertility, and work continues to refine its potency and duration.A special feeder could protect red squirrelsDelivering the contraceptive only to grey squirrels is one of the project's biggest challenges. Researchers are developing a species-selective hopper that opens only for animals above a set body weight. Weight data gathered by the Animal and Plant Health Agency showed that a 450g threshold would exclude every red squirrel measured while admitting more than 90% of grey squirrels. Trials of feeders with a weighted plate are being carried out in areas where both species live.The treatment is still being testedThe contraceptive is not yet a routine method of controlling grey squirrels in Britain. The project remains in research and development, with scientists still assessing how reliably it reduces fertility and whether it can be delivered without affecting other wildlife. Researchers are therefore developing the contraceptive and its delivery system side by side.The plan could complement existing control methodsFertility control is being explored as an additional tool rather than an immediate replacement for existing management. Traditional control removes animals from specific areas, while contraception would reduce the number of new animals being born. Lane said that combining a contraceptive with standard control methods is much more effective at bringing grey squirrel numbers down. For red squirrel conservationists, fewer greys in key habitats would mean less competition and a lower risk of squirrelpox transmission, giving isolated red populations a better chance of survival.You use AI every day. articles.title: Julianne Moore manifested her dreamy Manhattan duplex
articles.summary: The actor’s new two-bedroom West Village apartment is the home she’s always dreamt of.
articles.body: Julianne Moore’s apartment, a two-bedroom duplex smack in the center of New York’s West Village, was one she always wanted. “I had spotted it when I was wandering,” she confessed to Architectural Digest ahead of their November issue. A subconscious manifestation, perhaps. Today, she shares the space — which sits on top a 1920s building originally constructed as a residential hotel — with her film director husband Bart Freundlich. But even such a light-filled, serene apartment with impeccable city views still needed an eight-month renovation — according to Moore’s standards. She is passionate about design, after all. “Most of the changes we made were cosmetic,” said architectural designer and Moore’s brother-in-law Oliver Freundlich, who worked with her on the renovation — the sixth project the duo has taken on together. The pair “did a lot of editing,” he said, like installing a pantry for the kitchen, fitting a closet in the bedroom, and furnishing with both pre-owned and newly bought pieces. French mid-century chairs purchased in Paris in 1995 now live in the kitchen, vintage Anglepoise lamps sit atop bedside tables, and vintage tortoise shells hang from the library walls. “The trick was to make the place functional but without losing any of the magic,” said Freundlich. They therefore made resourceful decisions, like putting up shades made from fabric once used for curtains and leaving enough floor space for Moore to practice her beloved yoga. As an actor, Moore has played characters whose jobs have ranged from a linguistics professor in “Still Alice” (2014) to a horse trainer in “Echo Valley” (2025). In her most recent role in Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” Moore portrays a housewife who struggles as a method actor after being cast a small part at her local community theatre. It is an ironic role, given the Academy Award discreetly tucked away on a shelf in her library. If anything, she’s more suited to play an amateur interior designer. “Believe me, Julie scrutinized every switch and knob,” said Freundlich. “My taste is consistent, though it has evolved,” Moore told AD. Designing her new home was a playground for her creativity. “I love modernism. But this apartment is prewar, and you have to address that,” she added. “It’s not tiny, but it’s not massive, either, so materials and choices become even more important.” Her West Village town house, which had a beautiful garden that was featured in AD twice (March 2012 and November 2017), was more grand than her duplex’s terraces. Yet, the city views from her new outdoor space — of water towers, decorative brick and tilework, arches and columns and rooftop gardens — help soften the transition. The plan to downsize was fueled in part by this point in Moore’s life and career, with an emptying nest and — and unlike many other well-known actors — her commitment to be an engaged downtown New Yorker. “Lives change,” she said. Plus, her big holiday house in Montauk freed her from the need for a larger compound in the city. The result? “It feels very serene here,” she said of her new home in the midst of the metropolis. “I wanted a sense of history, of time, of all the people who have lived here before us. We’re just passing through. That’s the magic of New York City.”

Making the home functional was a priority for both Moore and Freundlich.

articles.title: ‘King of Injustice’: Golden naked Trump statue installed at European Parliament
articles.summary: Inside the European Parliament, politicians are now confronted with a grotesque vision of American power: an 8.5-foot-tall statue of President Donald Trump, naked but for a thin layer of 23-karat gold leaf.
articles.body: At a busy thoroughfare inside the European Parliament, passing politicians are now confronted with a grotesque and gilded vision of American power: an 8.5-foot-tall statue of President Donald Trump, naked but for a thin layer of 23-karat gold leaf. “Trump likes gold,” said Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, the statue’s creator, over the phone after it was unveiled Tuesday. “In a way, I think he would like this sculpture.” Titled “The Orange Plague,” the artwork has been installed in Strasbourg, France, the official seat of the European Parliament. The copper sculpture, also dubbed the “King of Injustice,” imagines the US president on the shoulders of a frail smaller figure. His thighs and sagging belly wrap tightly around the man’s head; his hands clutch at a long golf club and the scales of justice. “I am sitting on the back of a man,” reads the text on the statue’s plinth. “He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except step down from his back.” For Galschiøt, the work symbolizes what he sees as the US president’s threats to the environment and the rules-based world order. “Trump is destroying all the things I believe in,” he said. This is not necessarily a rebuke from the European Union, but rather from Danish politician Per Clausen, who sponsored the exhibit. Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) are entitled to host displays on parliament grounds, though all exhibitions must be approved by officials. Parliamentary rules prohibit events or exhibitions deemed “offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded,” or those that “undermine the dignity of Parliament.” Permission is not tantamount to explicit endorsement of their contents. Nonetheless Galschiøt, who had feared the application would be rejected, considers the green-light to be a form of tacit approval from Europe’s parliamentarians. “I think a lot of American people say, ‘OK, this is our president, but he’s also ridiculous in a way.’ And I think most Europeans see him like that, too,” he said. Galschiøt is known for provocative political artworks including the “Pillar of Shame,” a memorial to victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre that was controversially removed from a Hong Kong university in 2021. He said his decision to depict Trump naked alludes to Hans Christian Andersen’s story “The Emperor’s New Clothes,” in which a vain emperor parades the city in the nude. “Dictators don’t like you laughing at them,” he explained. The most recent temporary display is expected to remain on show until Thursday. It is accompanied by over 1,000 3D-printed miniatures of the sculpture, which are being made available to passersby as “protest tokens.” Clausen, the exhibition’s sponsor, is a member of Denmark’s socialist Red-Green Alliance party. Elected as an MEP in 2024, he is a member of The Left, a minority left-wing group representing around 6% of seats in the European Parliament. “I think we need to have a discussion about power in the world and how this power is used,” he said on the phone from Strasbourg. “The way Trump acts is a very, very big problem for people in Europe. I want to raise the discussion in Europe about how we can make our self-defense against Trump, and how can we make politics that is not dependent on him.” Aside from “some people from the extreme right wing,” Clausen said the response to the statue has been positive. “It’s very important that we in parliament have this opportunity to show things that not everybody agrees with.” Galschiøt has exhibited “The Orange Plague” in public several times before, including at the Munich Security Conference and last November’s COP30 UN climate conference in Brazil. He also plans to display it at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey next month. Trump is yet to comment on the artwork. A spokesperson for the European Parliament’s press service said via email that the exhibit was approved by the parliament’s quaestors, a cross-party group of MEP’s responsible for administrative matters. “Each MEP is entitled to sponsor two cultural events or exhibitions per parliamentary term in dedicated areas,” the statement added, adding that quaestors “assess the compliance with the rules in place.” In 2024, Galschiøt exhibited a model of his “Pillar of Shame” in front of the European Parliament building in Brussels as part of an exhibition of “forbidden art.” Then sponsored by another Danish MEP, Kira Marie Peter-Hansenm, the display took aim at Hong Kong and mainland China, where references to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre are heavily censored. The artist drew parallels between his most famous work and his latest swipe at Trump. “This is about the powerful and the powerless, and in a way, the ‘Pillar of Shame’ is also that.”

articles.title: King Charles and Elton John in the audience for Apple music workshop
articles.summary: Charles and Sir Elton visit an Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs music event offering industry skills to young people.
articles.body:
King Charles has visited a hi-tech music workshop for young people, in a collaboration between his King's Trust charity and technology firm Apple.

Pop royalty, in the form of Sir Elton John, was a special guest at the event, sitting beside the King, as they listened to a short performance from singer-songwriter Skye Newman.

The event was held at a music hall in Apple's headquarters building, in the restored Battersea Power Station in south west London.

The project being backed by the King is intended to equip young people with practical skills to work in the creative industries.

The King was introduced to Prophet Guillory, Apple Music's head of artist services, tools and community, who was praised for his work as a mentor for young people.

"Wow, you did your homework," Prophet said, when the King seemed familiar with his efforts.

The King was introduced to young performers at the event.

Another young musician said the problem was getting the money together to launch creative ideas.

Young performer Skye Newman faced what must have seemed like a very unusual X-Factor style panel - King Charles, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish and Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook.

The music workshop was part of a project between Apple and the King's Trust Creative Labs, and is the latest link-up between the royals and the Californian tech giant.

Last year, the King revealed a playlist of 17 of his favourite tracks , which was issued on Apple Music.

The King didn't include Sir Elton John in any of those choices - but the pop star has been a long-time supporter of the King's Trust charity, which was previously known as the Prince's Trust.

Now in its 50th year , the charity was set up to give opportunities to deprived and marginalised young people - and has so far helped 1.3 million people across the UK.

The tie-up with Apple shows the changing demands for work skills, including using the latest technology for young people wanting to build careers in the music and creative industries.

There was also a royal link with Battersea Power Station - as that had once provided the electricity for Buckingham Palace.

In the power station's control room, the link to the Palace had been discreetly labelled as "Carnaby Street", in case any intruders had ever been tempted to switch off the Palace lights.

articles.title: French leaders say they’re listening to students. Will it be enough?
articles.summary: After a heavy-handed response to the student protests sweeping France, the government has changed tack.
articles.body: After a heavy-handed response to the student protests sweeping France, the government has changed tack. It has banned police from using stun grenades after a student’s hand was blown off earlier in the week and there are promises to listen more to protesters’ demands. But with hundreds of schools still facing blockade and calls for more protests, will it be enough? What has the government said? “Empathy” and a little more “pedagogy” is what French President Emmanuel Macron demanded of police forces facing student protesters, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, following a massive day of protests on Tuesday. “The president recalled the necessity to maintain order, intervene each time there’s serious violence, all while asking us to act with the greatest proportionality,” Nunez told radio station RTL Wednesday, after an emergency ministerial meeting. Nunez, a former chief of Paris’ police, said that he had ordered forces to refrain from using the type of stun grenade linked to a teenager losing his hand in protests on Monday. “We don’t deal with a movement of highschoolers like we deal with a movement of adults,” Nunez said. France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told lawmakers Tuesday that high schools would replace lessons until the end of the week with a “period of internal democracy” to air grievances and discuss solutions. While refuting any suggestion of police repression, Lecornu condemned violence on the margins of protests, which were mostly peaceful Tuesday, despite the dramatic scenes that dominated coverage. Lecornu is due to address the French nation on Wednesday evening. The proposal for discussion is a tried and tested tactic of Macron, who has historically favored attempts to integrate public debate into policy making. His government tried to calm the Yellow Vests protests with a similar listening campaign in 2019. Meanwhile, 18 investigations into officers’ conduct during the protests have been opened by police internal investigators, Nunez said, adding they would examine the proportionality of police actions. Police forces “are there to protect the high schoolers,” he said. Are protests getting worse? On Wednesday, more than 500 educational institutions were due to be partially or fully closed because of blockades – a 41% decrease from Tuesday, according to the education ministry. That will leave 86% of schools open, the ministry added. According to the interior ministry, 488 people were detained around the high school protests Tuesday. The student blockade actions on Wednesday were a fraction of the hundreds of thousands who marched with workers’ unions Tuesday in support of students across France. But it’s a sign of the rancor among students that protests are continuing day-to-day. Student unions have called for a day of protests on October 17 and five major teaching unions said they would strike Thursday in solidarity with their students, with little sign that school blockades will halt in the meantime. What do students want? More teachers, smaller class sizes and buildings better adapted to the climate are the most common demands of high school protesters. Student union leaders, who represent some of the young people protesting, have also called for a 10-billion-euro ($11.2-billion) investment in high school and university-level education. A 10-point list of proposals drawn up by student unions included rethinking student workloads, ending a controversial university admissions system, ending police violence against students and creating more student accommodation. Sabrine Kharbach, spokesperson of the Student Union federation of unionized students, told BFMTV that blockades would continue until their demands were met. Anaïs Ella, spokesperson for Les Lycéens, a student association, told CNN that Lecornu didn’t address the demands laid out by student unions. She said that some of the prime minister’s proposals – including filling teaching posts in exam-year classes – “was the basics of the education system.” She said that money would solve some of their demands but that a deeper reset in relations between the government and students was needed. “We are the ones most directly affected by the national education system, yet we aren’t actually listened to,” she added. Since the weekend, there have been concerted efforts among students to reject the violence that has marred protests. Student Angelo Via, 19, who protested in the street Tuesday, told CNN there was a feeling of “powerlessness” in the face of violent police actions, despite many students protesting peacefully. He hopes the protests will bring about “radical change,” especially regarding education budgets. What’s next? There will be relief in France at the interior minister’s decision to ban one type of police grenade, as the injuries suffered by some teenage protesters has sparked widespread horror. But the proposal for time for debate has been met with skepticism in some quarters. The main union for school directors, SNPDEN-UNSA, said that the single day set aside for discussions was insufficient to respond to problems in depth. Nicolas Bonnet, national secretary of the union, told BFMTV that, “something other than a mere consultation period was required to get out of this crisis.” There are whispers in France of these protests transforming into another Yellow Vests movement, which was leaderless, nationwide and unified a broad church of grievances. Mimicking the months-long violent protests – the longest in French history – that rocked Macron’s first term, students and journalists have already begun referring to the next day of protest set for Thursday as “Act IV.” Additional reporting by Lucie Lepellec and Lisa Courbebaisse.

articles.title: Man who murdered ex-partner after his prison release is jailed
articles.summary: Robert Sabat is given a 17-year-minimum jail term for the fatal stabbing of his former partner.
articles.body:
A violent offender who was released from jail the day after he was sentenced stabbed his former partner and then begged to be returned to prison because he was going to "go on a murder spree", the Old Bailey has heard.

Robert Sabat, 60, pleaded guilty to murdering 42-year-old mother-of-two Dickiesha Nurse, who he stabbed at her flat in Tulse Hill, south London, last October.

He had been released on licence from HMP Wandsworth on 17 October 2025 after being sentenced the day before to a 12-month jail term for possession of a bladed article and harassment. He had been in prison on remand since May 2025 when he was freed.

Sabat, of Balham, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years.

When he was released in October 2025, Sabat had served 40% of his 12-month sentence instead of the previous 50% requirement, in line with the government's change to offenders' automatic release dates, which began the month before .

Last week, the Sentencing Act 2026 replaced this policy and some prisoners can now be released after they have served a third of their sentence.

When he was arrested on suspicion of Nurse's murder, Sabat claimed he had killed before and was planning a "murder spree".

He told officers: "I'm a murderer, I don't want to come back out, I wanna go to jail... I've been let out a week.

"Let me back... I'm happy in there, I've done wrong. I killed before and got away with it.

"I've murdered three people so far. I'm gonna go on a murder spree."

Outlining the facts of the case, prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Sabat and Nurse had been in a relationship and had known each other for many years as the defendant was brought up by her father.

Two days after Sabat was released from prison, Nurse's children visited her and on returning home, told their father her "friend or cousin" had been there.

On 22 October, Nurse told a neighbour Sabat was at her address and would not leave. Another neighbour saw her in the street shouting: "Get out of my house."

Two days later, a neighbour heard a single scream coming from the victim's home, the court heard.

Nurse was last seen on CCTV on 25 October. Her children tried to visit the following day but got no response when they knocked on her door.

Her family raised concerns on 27 October and paramedics entered the flat, where the defendant, armed with a knife, charged at a paramedic, the court heard.

The London Ambulance Service crew and family members withdrew from the property and police were called, Farrelly said.

Soon after, armed officers forced entry to the property and used Tasers as they detained Sabat.

Farrelly said officers found Nurse on a bed with a pillow over her face and with multiple stab wounds to the face. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A post-mortem examination found she had sustained about eight stab wounds, including to the left side of her face, neck and hands.

Police recovered from the flat a knife with Nurse's blood on it, a bag marked "HMP valuables" and prison records in Sabat's name.

In mitigation, Alisdair Williamson KC said Sabat had lived "on the margins" with spells in jail and had struggled with his mental health, depression and anxiety.

In a victim impact statement, Nurse's sister Samantha Carvalho described Sabat as a "menace to society", and said the "heartlessness" of the killing was "impossible to comprehend".

Her mother Claudette McBean described her daughter as kind, loving and the "life and soul of the party".

Farrelly said the defendant had convictions dating back to 1987, including for burglary, assault, wounding with intent, knife possession, and harassment of an ex-partner.

In 2013, he was made subject to a non-molestation order of a former partner and in August 2023 he was given a restraining order after being cleared of attempted murder after the complainant – his landlady – failed to attend court.

articles.title: Wildfire-fighting crews in Berkshire sent without proper PPE, says CLA
articles.summary: The Country Land and Business Association calls for more support for firefighters tacking wildfires.
articles.body:
Crews are being sent to tackle wildfires without proper protective gear, a group that represents rural land owners and businesses has claimed.

The Country Land and Business Association (CLA) said a Freedom of Information request (FOI) showed that Royal Berkshire Fire and Rescue Service (RBFRS) had no specialist wildfire PPE or any drones.

CLA president Gavin Lane said some firefighters were "being sent into wildfires in heavy kit made for burning buildings, worn for hours across open ground in summer heat".

RBFRS said it would continue to ensure its firefighters "have the training, equipment and support they need".

Earlier this year, RBFRS revealed it had already responded to more than 250 fires in the open this year , several of which were classed as wildfires.

According to CLA's findings that was "a five-year record in just the first six months of 2026".

RBFRS said the continued hot and dry weather "meant we responded to a further 295 vegetation fires between July and September, including 32 wildfires", according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

The CLA said that 12 out of 22 fire services that responded to its FOI had "no specialist wildfire PPE, despite repeated warnings from fire services that standard PPE can be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions".

"This can cause crews to overheat, or remove PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation," it said.

"In Berkshire, where wait times for wildfires specifically were provided, just 16% of all wildfires were attended in the target time, with crews taking as long as 43 minutes to arrive at the scene."

To tackle this issue, the CLA is calling for "more funding, resources and equipment for fire services".

"And government must lift the ban on controlled burning, so landowners have the freedom to reduce fuel loads before a blaze becomes a disaster," Lane added.

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

RBFRS said it took the risk of wildfires "extremely seriously" and the safety of its firefighters remained "a top priority".

"In the first six months of 2026, appliance availability remained strong and we maintained our commitment to providing a baseline of 14 frontline fire engines for Berkshire," it added.

"We have also continued to strengthen our wildfire capability through specialist training, dedicated 4×4 wildfire units and enhanced officer expertise to support the safe and effective management of complex incidents."

articles.title: Okinawa governor urges Japan action after US Marine arrested over killing
articles.summary: Growing anger after US Marine Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39.
articles.body:
The governor of Okinawa has demanded that Japan’s central government do more to ensure effective discipline among United States service members on the southern island following the arrest of a US Marine on accusations that he robbed and murdered a local woman.

Governor Genta Koja, in Tokyo for the first time since taking office a week ago, conveyed on Wednesday Okinawa’s outrage in his meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, asking her government for further efforts to reduce the burden of hosting US military bases on the small island.

“Okinawa has requested preventive measures every time similar crimes were repeated in past, and now we have this case again,” Koja told Takaichi at the Prime Minister’s Office on Wednesday.

“I must say past disciplinary measures and human rights education implemented by the US military have not worked at all,” Koja said.

People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy US military presence on the island and complained about noise, pollution and crime related to bases used by US forces.

Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested over the weekend on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.

The US military in Okinawa earlier announced a 48-hour pause of all military operations for training through Friday, as well as restrictions on the ability of troops to leave their base and a ban on the consumption of alcohol.

Benjamin T Watson, the Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said that the 48-hour period would give commanders the time to lead training with all service members on “standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community”.

The lieutenant general, the most senior US military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day “period of reflection” beginning Friday.

“During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500,” Watson said.

Takaichi said she regretted the “heinous crime” and shared the outrage.

Noting the new disciplinary measures announced by the US military, Takaichi said she expected the US government to take subsequent steps.

Japan and the US will discuss “how to implement preventive measures that are effective”, she said.

The presence of US troops in Okinawa has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct ‌‌of personnel.

Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine convicted of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.

In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.

The same year, US Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

articles.title: FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott rings Nasdaq Closing Bell as network celebrates 30th anniversary
articles.summary: Suzanne Scott rang the Nasdaq Closing Bell surrounded by longtime colleagues as Fox News Channel celebrates its remarkable 30th anniversary.
articles.body: FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott rang the Closing Bell on Tuesday at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City as the company celebrates Fox News Channel’s 30th anniversary. Fox News Channel debuted on Oct. 7, 1996, and original hosts Lauren Green, Trace Gallagher, Steve Doocy and Brit Hume were in attendance, alongside FOX News Media President and Executive Editor Jay Wallace and other 30-year employees who are now at the executive level, to help Scott celebrate three decades since they helped launch the network. "It's a tremendous honor to be here at Nasdaq as we celebrate a remarkable milestone, 30 years of Fox News," Scott said when delivering remarks before ringing the bell. LAUREN GREEN: I WAS FOX NEWS CHANNEL'S FIRST ON-AIR HIRE. HERE'S HOW A DREAM BECAME A POWERHOUSE "Three decades ago, Fox Corporation Chairman Emeritus Rupert Murdoch launched Fox News with an ambitious idea to give audiences another voice in the national conversation and to build a news organization that provided balance to all Americans," Scott continued. "Thirty years later, his vision has grown from one linear network to a multi-platform powerhouse of digital, streaming, audio, books and beyond, made possible by the leadership of Fox Corp Executive Chair and Chief Executive Officer Lachlan Murdoch." Scott noted that FOX News Media platforms have an enduring connection with the audience and reach over 200 million people on a monthly basis. "Milestones like this are about recognizing the people behind our success, the journalists, producers, technicians, correspondents, executives, and countless colleagues who show up every day with inspiring skill, energy, determination, and a genuine commitment to their craft," Scott said. "And they are about the viewers who have welcomed Fox News Channel into their homes, their workplaces, and their daily lives as we meet them wherever they are," Scott added. "So today, as we celebrate 30 years of stories reported and analyzed, and history witnessed at each turn, we also look ahead because the next chapter of media is being shaped right now by new technology, new platforms, and new ways of connecting with audiences." DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE Scott, who joined Fox News in its inaugural year of 1996 and was recently inducted into the Broadcasting+Cable Hall of Fame, held several production and creative positions before taking over as CEO in 2018. Under her leadership, Fox News has dominated cable ratings and regularly beats broadcast networks. "On behalf of everyone at Fox News Media, thank you to all of our viewers and to all of our colleagues who made all of this possible. And now, with great pride and gratitude, we celebrate 30 years of Fox News Channel," Scott said to wrap up her remarks. 'THE FIVE' LEADS CABLE NEWS FOR 20TH STRAIGHT QUARTER AS FOX NEWS OUTDRAWS CNN AND MS NOW COMBINED Scott was then surrounded by longtime colleagues to officially halt transactions for the day as Fox News-themed red, white and blue confetti rained down. The iconic Closing Bell, which ends market trading, has been rung by influential figures ranging from Jeff Bezos and Oprah Winfrey to Michael Jordan. Nasdaq Executive Vice President Jeff Thomas presented Scott with a Closing Bell crystal prior to the ceremony, calling FOX News Media "one of the most recognized and influential media brands in the world." As part of Scott’s ongoing efforts to expand across platforms, Scott launched FOX News Books in 2020 and also spearheaded the brand refresh of FOX News Digital, FOX News Audio and FOX Business. articles.summary: Sebastian Burley, 36, finished the 26.2-mile course in 4:00:33 on Sunday, 26 April 2026, becoming the fastest man to complete a marathon in a full-body
articles.body: Sebastian Burley, 36, finished the 26.2-mile course in 4:00:33 on Sunday, 26 April 2026, becoming the fastest man to complete a marathon in a full-body inflatable costume, according to Guinness World Records. Burley ran to raise money for Action for Children, a charity that protects and supports vulnerable children and young people. When The Voice reported on his run on 28 April, he had raised £2,132. Burley said the costume became incredibly hot and humid, with nowhere for the heat to escape, and that it was difficult to breathe in, let alone run in. He chose the charity partly because, as a father, he was concerned about children living in poverty. His was 1 of 38 Guinness World Records titles set or broken by participants at the 2026 London Marathon.Seb Burley London Marathon 2026: Goonhavern runner sets Guinness World Record in chicken costumeThe 2026 London Marathon was the 46th edition of the race, and Guinness World Records says 38 record titles were set or broken at the 2026 London Marathon, involving 39 record holders. Guinness says 38 record titles were set or broken during the marathon, with 39 record holders. The records covered a wide range of categories, including costume-based attempts and challenges involving different types of clothing and equipment. Burley's record appears on Guinness's official record page as the fastest marathon in a full-body inflatable costume by a male, with a time of 4:00:33. The record was achieved at the TCS London Marathon in London on 26 April 2026. Other 2026 record holders included Keyur Gudka, who ran the marathon in traditional Indian dress in 3:08:10, Simon Fannon, who knitted a 5.59-metre scarf while running in 5:48:08, and Sabastian Sawe, who set the men's marathon record with a time of 1:59:30.The 2026 list also included records for runners dressed as a three-dimensional toy, a firefighter, a camera, a clown, an electrical engineer and a sweet food, among other categories. Guinness says the London Marathon has worked with the organisation for almost 2 decades, giving runners the opportunity to attempt records while also supporting fundraising efforts.Fastest marathon in a full-body inflatable costume: how Burley’s 4:00:33 comparesBurley’s 4:00:33 translates to approximately 9 minutes 10 seconds per mile, or about 5 minutes 42 seconds per kilometre. A pre-race listing identified Arnie Delstanche as the record holder with a time of 4:07:46, meaning Burley’s finish was 7 minutes and 13 seconds faster. The physical challenge was not simply the distance. Before the marathon, Burley had described the inflatable chicken costume as becoming extremely hot and humid inside. He also said that running in windy conditions felt like running with a parachute. He had previously run in the chicken costume and was preparing to attempt the record while raising money for Action for Children. After completing the race, Burley again described the conditions inside the costume as difficult, telling The Voice: “The costume got incredibly hot and humid inside and there was nowhere for the heat and humidity to go.” He added that it was difficult to breathe in, let alone run in.Action for Children fundraising: why Burley ran the London Marathon for vulnerable childrenBurley was raising money for Action for Children, which supports children and young people through services and other forms of support. The Voice reported that he had raised £2,132 by 28 April, 2 days after the marathon. Because the amount was reported at that point in time, the total could have changed after the newspaper's report. Burley said before the marathon that he chose Action for Children partly because a close family member works for the charity. His reference to 4.5 million children reflected the government's earlier FYE 2024 estimate for relatively low income after housing costs. The latest HBAI statistics, which use an updated approach to administrative data, put the FYE 2025 figure at 4.0 million.The government's July 2026 projections estimate that 3.6 million children will be in relative low income after housing costs in the financial year ending 2030. That represents a projected reduction of 400,000 children from the FYE 2025 level. The Department for Work and Pensions stresses that these are projections under specific policy and economic assumptions, rather than forecasts of what will necessarily happen. For Burley, the marathon combined a demanding physical challenge with his fundraising goal. articles.title: Millions of Pakistanis get government fuel relief but some miss out
articles.summary: Pakistan has subsidised petrol for millions, but some economists caution that those most needing help are left out.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – More than 9.5 million people have received subsidised petrol under a special fuel relief scheme launched by Pakistan’s prime minister, Federal Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja told Al Jazeera on Wednesday.

The initiative, aimed at lower-income citizens, comes as the government attempts to help households deal with fuel price increases tied to the war on Iran.

The scheme, launched in September, offers 100 rupees ($0.36) off every litre of petrol to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and small cars, through a text-message system.

Petrol prices have risen by nearly 50 percent since the war began on February 28, adding to Pakistan’s economic hardship and putting further pressure on consumers already grappling with rising inflation.

Explaining the process, Khawaja, the minister for information technology and telecommunications, said applicants text their national ID number, vehicle registration, and province to 9771. A second message, sent before each visit to a pump, generates a token redeemable anywhere in the country.

Two- and three-wheelers get 500 rupees ($1.80) a week, capped at four tokens a month. Cars with engines of up to 800cc get 1,000 rupees ($3.60) every 10 days, for three tokens monthly.

After complaints, registration, once a paid service, was made free, and a five-litre minimum purchase was scrapped for the same reason.

Khawaja told Al Jazeera the system had been redesigned based on experiences of users on the ground.

Riders no longer need the vehicle to be registered in their own name, as long as they can supply the exact registration date shown on the documents.

“Even in my own house, there’s a bike registered in our name that our cook uses for daily errands,” Khawaja said, explaining why the ownership requirement for two- and three-wheelers was dropped on September 20.

An earlier cash-transfer scheme in April had reached just over a million bike owners, she said, largely because disbursement required a bank account most riders did not have.

Government officials say that the scheme has been expanded to include wider sections of society, especially those who depend on their vehicles to generate income.

“There’s a benefit; it’s not like there’s nothing,” Shakeel Ahmed, 45, an electrician in Islamabad, told Al Jazeera. “The relief is decent for people who use it normally, for local trips. But for people like us, who put in 1,000 to 1,500 rupees [$3.60-$5.40] of petrol a day, it’s not enough.”

Safiya Aftab, an economist, told Al Jazeera the scheme has reached the people it was meant to.

“The scheme has indeed reached low-income segments of society, people who typically use two-wheelers and 800cc cars. So yes, it’s a good thing that they are subsidising the poor,” she said.

Aftab, however, also pointed to a levy – 114 rupees ($0.41) for every litre – that the government charges. This, she said, was helping the government raise revenue. She said the government is now earning more than 100 billion rupees ($361m) a month from the levy, which is fuelling inflation.

“The levy was originally meant as a sort of environmental tax, to discourage the use of petrol. Now it has become a full revenue earner for the government, one that helps keep the fiscal deficit down,” the economist said.

The Pakistani government has approved 75 billion rupees ($271m) for the scheme’s first three months, through November.

Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik put the running cost at 25-30 billion rupees ($90m-$108m) a month at launch. By late September, he said, it had risen to 35-40 billion rupees ($126m-$144m).

Malik has said the government is prepared to run the scheme for up to 10 months, or “until the end of the war”, if needed.

Pakistan is currently under a $7bn International Monetary Fund programme, and an IMF team is in Islamabad this week for talks with the government as it seeks to keep its fiscal commitments on track while responding to the fuel shock.

Officials familiar with the government’s talks with the IMF say the Fund wants relief capped at three months and routed instead through the Benazir Income Support Programme, the country’s main cash-transfer scheme.

Khawaja said the IMF’s position from the outset was that relief had to be targeted, not universal, which was why the scheme was built around actual token use rather than a blanket price cut.

But there are claims that the relief is not reaching all. Cars with engines larger than 800cc, diesel vehicles and public transport are excluded entirely, leading some experts to suggest that the subsidy scheme risks missing the most vulnerable sections of Pakistani society.

“A poor household that uses public transport, walks to work, or relies on diesel-powered transport may receive nothing while still facing higher food and transport costs,” Khaqan Najeeb, a former adviser in Pakistan’s Ministry of Finance, told Al Jazeera.

More than 8.1 million tokens had gone to two- and three-wheelers by late September, compared with fewer than 380,000 for cars, Malik said. A November 2024 Gallup Pakistan survey found that 79 percent of respondents, in rural and urban areas alike, said they use public transport such as buses or wagons.

At 100 rupees a litre, the maximum monthly saving is 2,000 rupees ($7.20) for a motorcycle user and 3,000 rupees ($10.80) for an eligible car owner, Najeeb said, calling it “useful household relief, but not enough to offset the broader cost-of-living shock”.

Petrol has climbed from 266 rupees ($0.96) a litre before the war to nearly 395 rupees ($1.42), despite a partial rollback in April. Inflation rose to 10.3 percent in September from 7 percent in February, Najeeb said.

Sajid Amin Javed, a senior economist at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute in Islamabad, said the relief was “minimal”, but added that this was understandable given the IMF constraints on Pakistan.

“The relief is minimal, and that is understandable as we are in an IMF programme,” Javed told Al Jazeera, arguing that cutting the petroleum development levy, which still adds 114 rupees to every litre, would deliver broader relief than a capped subsidy.

“The government is using the petroleum development levy to fill its revenue gap, but that comes at a significant cost in terms of inflation, growth and household welfare,” Javed said.

Najeeb, however, argued the scheme should not become a permanent fixture of Pakistan’s energy policy – and should be used only to make oil price shocks “less damaging”.

articles.title: Detained immigrants at US ICE facility launch hunger strike over prolonged detention
articles.summary: A group of at least 73 immigrants detained at a privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Georgia has launched a hunger strike,
articles.body: A group of at least 73 immigrants detained at a privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Georgia has launched a hunger strike, protesting prolonged detention and alleged poor conditions inside the centre, according to advocates and family members.The hunger strike began Tuesday at the Folkston D Ray James ICE Processing Center in south-east Georgia, which is operated by private prison company GEO Group under a contract with ICE. The facility, a former state prison, currently houses around 2,200 detainees, according to the latest ICE data cited by the Guardian.The protesters, most of whom are asylum seekers, are demanding their release while their immigration and asylum cases continue through the US court system.Georgia ICE detainees demand release, family reunificationThe protesters published an open letter signed by 45 detained men, some of whom have been held at the facility since October 2023. They have called on Congress, judges, advocacy groups and the public to highlight their cases and urged ICE to release them.The group is also seeking protection from re-detention and deportation, as well as reunification with their families.The letter said many detainees had spent between 16 months and nearly three years in detention despite not being accused of a crime. The signatories said prolonged detention without an individual assessment of whether a person is dangerous or likely to flee raised questions about fairness."We come from different countries, races, believes [sic], and background, but we share one thing in common," the detainees said in the letter, adding that they came to the US seeking protection.The hunger strike involves detainees from several countries, including Russia, China, Sudan, Afghanistan, Nepal and others.One of the organisers, Russian asylum seeker Idris Makhmudov, was reportedly placed in solitary confinement this week, according to Monica Whatley of the Campaign to Shut Down the Folkston ICE Processing Center.Detainees allege poor medical care, moldy foodTwo Russian detainees, Alexey Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov, have also released a nine-page report detailing what they described as poor conditions at the facility.Their allegations include inadequate medical and dental care, unhealthy or spoiled food, cramped and noisy living quarters, limited access to sunlight and fresh air, and difficulty communicating with ICE officials.The report also accused some GEO Group employees of hostile and xenophobic behaviour and alleged that detainees were threatened with solitary confinement.A detainee from Yemen who is taking part in the hunger strike is suffering from lung cancer and has a US citizen child, advocates said.GEO Group referred questions about the allegations to ICE. The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not respond to detailed requests for comment.The protest is the latest hunger strike at an ICE detention facility since the Trump administration returned to office. Earlier this year, detainees at the GEO Group-operated Delaney Hall facility in New Jersey also staged a hunger strike over detention conditions.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: From 'vote chori' to 'chita andolan': Street protests return with a new playbook
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Slogans are ringing out, crowds are turning up and the streets are once again abuzz with protests.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Slogans are ringing out, crowds are turning up and the streets are once again abuzz with protests.On Tuesday, INDIA bloc MPs took their protest against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls to the national capital, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. The march took an unexpected turn when Rahul Gandhi surprised the police with a last-minute change of course, turning it into a sit-in.A day later, opposition MPs were back with another dramatic flash protest on Janpath streets, where Priyanka Gandhi Vadra lay down on the road and refused to budge until the CEC agreed to meet opposition leaders.And more could be coming. Cockroach Janata Party’s Abhijeet Dipke, who rallied young protesters during the anti-NEET paper leak agitation in July, has warned of a “Jantar Mantar 2.0” on October 10 if the CEC does not resign.But Delhi is not the only place, and politicians are not the only ones taking their grievances to the streets. Across the country, protests over very different issues are bringing people out in an attempt to make their voices heard.The protests differ in scale, issue and leadership. But together, they point to something familiar returning to the foreground: street politics.The street has always been a political stagePeaceful protests have always been a part of our democracy. India's politics has rarely been confined to Parliament, party offices or election rallies. The streets have always had a part to play.Mahatma Gandhi turned marches, boycotts and satyagraha into instruments of mass politics during the freedom struggle. Decades later, Jayaprakash Narayan's movement drew students and citizens onto the streets against the Indira Gandhi government.Anna Hazare's anti-corruption protests filled Jantar Mantar and Ramlila Maidan in 2011. The anti-CAA protests saw prolonged sit-ins, while farmers camped at Delhi's borders for more than a year before the three farm laws were repealed.How social media changed street mobilisationStreet politics, then, is hardly new. What keeps changing are the tools used to trigger, spread and sustain mobilisation. Political analyst Uday Chandra feels social media is making protests more visible while also changing who can start and sustain them."Social media certainly makes protests visible to millions, enabling a rapid or viral spread. But it also does something more important: it reduces dependence on political parties, unions and established organisations to mobilise people. A grievance may now turn into a movement before conventional political actors decide how to respond," Uday Chandra says.But the current round of protests goes beyond social-media amplification, feels Chandra."I think something real is happening beyond social-media amplification. Street protest never quite disappeared from politics in India, but for much of the past decade, electoral politics under a highly centralised party machinery overshadowed it. What we are seeing now is, to my mind, the re-emergence of the street as an autonomous political arena," he said.When the youth lead, parties followWhat stands out in this round of protests is not just the issues being raised, but who is often raising them first.On questions ranging from examinations to electoral rolls, young people have managed to create pressure outside the usual party machinery. Increasingly, political parties have found themselves responding aggressively to issues they did not start.So, have young people and students shown political parties the way back to street mobilisation? The events surrounding the NEET protests in July this year are a case in point.As students protested over the paper leak, Jantar Mantar became the centre of an agitation that continued for weeks. The CJP emerged as the pressure group leading the agitation and eventually ensuring the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Union education minister.Many political parties that initially stood on the sidelines scrambled to join the agitation. On July 21, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Mallikarjun Kharge and other opposition leaders staged a sit-in outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence over police action against students protesting the NEET paper leak.But Chandra argues that the CJP, as a movement, differs significantly from political parties and earlier large movements such as the Anna Hazare agitation or the farmers' protests."CJP is much more decentralised than the two movements you mention. The Anna movement had recognisable leaders and a national campaign/agenda. Likewise, the farmers’ protests rested on strong unions, local organisation, and the economic capacity to sustain mobilisation for months. By contrast, what we see emerging now is networked, relatively leader-light, and often issue-specific," he said.The CJP advantage is also organisational, he feels."Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube and other online platforms can connect previously unrelated groups rapidly. Mobilisation is, therefore, not only faster but more fluid. You do not necessarily need to build and register an organisation before launching a movement. Increasingly, the movement precedes the organisation," Chandra adds.It is perhaps this realisation that has forced political parties to course-correct their mobilisation strategies.Rahul Gandhi, who faced criticism for prioritising his "Chhatron ki Goonj" campaign instead of backing the anti-NEET protests led by CJP, has now made a more direct attempt to help Congress enter the protest space. On October 4, he launched the 'Satyagraha' portal, which seeks to map protests across the country and connect people agitating over different issues.For Chandra, the move shows that Congress has recognised the risks of ignoring protests that begin online and then spill onto the streets."The Satyagraha platform strikes me as an attempt to situate the INC within an emerging ecology of anti-BJP protests. This is an interesting shift in political organisation. It takes the party from a traditional top-heavy high command structure to a node connecting diverse and dispersed struggles against the status quo."Beyond Jantar Mantar: The protests away from the spotlightThe high-decibel protests against Gyanesh Kumar or over NEET are only one part of the story, perhaps the more visible one. Away from the national spotlight, peaceful protests have been taking place across the country over a wide range of issues.They may be small, localised and often unconnected: women’s safety, land, displacement, water, facilities in schools, local governance and more. But together, they show how the street remains an important space for people trying to make themselves heard.In Delhi, young women have marched over women's safety after cases of sexual violence. Demonstrations have also spread to cities including Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Patna and Dehradun, with protesters demanding safer public spaces and greater accountability from governments and police.In Madhya Pradesh’s Panna district, families affected by the Ken-Betwa river-linking project have revived their "Chita Andolan". Protesters have slept on funeral pyres, stood in water and gone on hunger strike over compensation and rehabilitation.In Maharashtra’s Maval, farmers opposing the Pavana closed pipeline project announced a 'jal samadhi' agitation while also demanding rehabilitation for families that surrendered land for the Pavana dam decades ago.Water has also brought farmers onto the streets in Karnataka, where organisations in Krishna basin districts have opposed releasing reservoir water to Telangana, arguing that drought-hit areas within Karnataka should be given priority.At IIT Bombay too, students have turned their protest over the death by suicide of student Sahil Wakode into a hunger strike, with the JNU Students’ Union joining calls for action on the demands raised by protesters.The scale and demands vary sharply. Some protests involve thousands; others are confined to a university campus, a few villages or even a handful of streets. They may target the Centre, state governments, local administrations or institutions, but the impulse is the same: take the grievance to the street.The street is old, the tools are changingSo, street politics is old, but the mobilisation techniques have changed. Earlier movements depended heavily on student organisations, unions, public meetings and, later, television coverage. Today, a protest can begin on Instagram or X before it reaches Jantar Mantar.Social media has also changed the language of protest. A slogan shouted on the street can become a meme within hours, while posters, one-liners, chants and songs travel far beyond the protest site.Recent demonstrations have offered plenty of examples. At women's protests in Delhi, slogans such as 'Ek kachori, do samosa, in mardon ka kya bharosa' quickly travelled from the street to Instagram reels, using humour and rhyme to make a serious point about women's safety and gender attitudes.At the Mumbai protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, placards carried lines such as 'Gyanu must go' and the Bollywood-inspired 'Vote churaya mera, kisne o sanam? Gyanu ne'. Days later, Rahul Gandhi carried the Gen Z-style message "Gyanesh, it's done bro!" during the INDIA bloc's march to the Election Commission. Whether it will culiminate into effective but what it definitely did was make people stop and notice.And Gen Z may not be the youngest generation learning to protest.In Lucknow, around 200 schoolgirls blocked a road in the rain over a shortage of teachers and a damaged road leading to their school. In Fatehpur, around 1,000 students staged a four-hour protest demanding drinking water and repairs to classrooms. In several cases, authorities acted after the protests.What has changed is not the instinct to protest, but how quickly a grievance can find an audience and become visible. The slogan may now become a meme and the mobilisation may begin on a phone screen. The destination, however, is often still the same: the street.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Peterborough cadet leader posed as girl on Snapchat, court hears
articles.summary: A former councillor goes on trial accused of 25 sexual offences, many involving children.
articles.body:
An Army Cadets instructor and former councillor posed as a teenage girl on the messaging app Snapchat to encourage boys to send him nude photos, a court has heard.

Rylan Ray, who was a detachment commander for the youth organisation in Peterborough, went on trial earlier accused of 25 sexual offences, many of them involving children.

The 26-year-old, of Westgate in the city, denies the charges.

Prosecutor Claire Matthews told Ipswich Crown Court that Ray had created a "fake persona of a teenage girl" to extract embarrassing photos from his alleged victims.

The charges include one count of rape, four of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, and three of making indecent images of children.

Offences are alleged to have happened over a six-year period and involve 11 male complainants, many of whom were cadets.

Ray also held positions at two schools in the Peterborough area and served as a local councillor, Matthews said.

"The roles he held inevitably commanded respect from those around him and they granted access to young people around him," the barrister told the jury.

His position meant he could "add cadets to WhatsApp" or other social media platforms to talk about their duties, Matthews explained.

"But in many instances he would use them to encourage them to engage in Snapchat conversations," she added.

"Where the communications would become sexual in nature."

One boy, who was aged between 13 and 14 when the alleged abuse took place, told police he felt like he had to comply with Ray's requests for explicit images.

"He would dump his mental health on me and said the only distraction from his mental health was me doing that," the teenager said in a police interview played to the court.

Matthews said several boys reported being contacted on Snapchat by a user purporting to be a girl named Chelsea, who sent intimate images of a female.

Some of the boys returned similar photos of themselves.

The IP address linked to the Snapchat account was traced back to Ray's home address, the prosecutor said.

"Also found on his handset was the icon used by Chelsea on her Snapchat account," she said.

"That was Chelsea," she added, pointing to Ray in the dock.

Matthews said Ray was asked in a police interview if he was Chelsea, to which he responded: "Not me, absolutely not."

The court was told inappropriate photos and videos of children were found on Ray's devices – including 73 of the most serious Category A classification.

Not everyone pictured had yet been identified.

Ray was first elected to represent Eye, Thorney and Newborough as a Conservative on Peterborough City Council in 2022 and more recently sat as an independent.

He did not stand for re-election in the May 2026 elections.

The trial, expected to last four weeks, continues.
